analysis.one_liner: Requires Congress to vote to approve every major federal regulation before it can take effect.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the Senate Homeland Security Committee without amendment in July 2020, was reported and placed on the Senate calendar in December 2020, and never received a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, federal agencies write and issue rules that carry the force of law — for example, limits on pollution, workplace hazards, or financial practices — and Congress can only cancel them by passing a resolution to do so. This bill would flip that: any rule affecting the economy by $100 million or more would have no effect at all unless both chambers of Congress passed, and the President signed, a law approving it. Critics pointed out that because Congress rarely passes anything, the practical effect would be that most big new rules — on air and water quality, workplace safety, consumer finance, and more — would die by default.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses facing costly federal rules. Any industry subject to a major rule — for example fossil fuel and chemical producers facing environmental standards, manufacturers facing workplace safety rules, or financial firms facing consumer-protection rules — would gain a practical veto, because a rule would only take effect if a divided Congress affirmatively passed it.

how_it_helps.text: Major rules — those with an annual economic effect of $100 million or more, major cost or price increases, or significant effects on competition or employment — could not take effect unless Congress enacted a joint resolution of approval within 70 session or legislative days; if not enacted, the rule is deemed not approved and never takes effect.

Agencies would have to publish the data, studies, and cost-benefit analyses behind each rule, and the Comptroller General would report to Congress on whether the rule imposes new mandates on private activity.

Emergency rules for imminent health or safety threats, criminal law enforcement, or national security could take effect for a 90-day period on the President's written determination, but the approval procedure would still run.
Nonmajor rules could take effect only if Congress did not pass a disapproval resolution, extending the existing congressional review process.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who rely on federal health, safety, environmental, and financial protections. Since Congress historically approves very few agency rules affirmatively, most major rules would be expected to fail, leaving pollution limits, workplace protections, and consumer safeguards unenforced unless lawmakers act.

drawbacks.text: The design favors inaction: because Congress seldom enacts any legislation, most major rules would simply expire by default, so the bill functions less as case-by-case oversight than as a near-blanket block on significant new regulation.

The burden would fall hardest on rules that protect people against concentrated harms — an agency could not act on a new hazard, pollutant, or financial abuse unless 535 legislators each affirmatively voted for a rule with no named beneficiaries.
The bill exempts monetary policy rules and lets hunting, fishing, and camping rules take effect at agencies' discretion, carving some areas out of the review it imposes elsewhere.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated goal — making Congress accountable for the content of the laws it passes — is a real constitutional argument, and the added transparency requirements for agency data have value on their own. But the mechanism is all-or-nothing: a rule either gets an affirmative act of Congress within 70 days or vanishes. Given how rarely Congress passes anything, the design would function as a de facto moratorium on major regulation, and the people who depend on those rules — for clean air and water, safe workplaces, and honest financial markets — would bear that cost while regulated industries gained an effective veto.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee for about a year and a half, got a favorable committee report in July 2020, was formally reported and placed on the Senate calendar in mid-December 2020 during the post-election session, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2021 without the Senate ever voting on it.

narrative.text: Rand Paul introduced the bill on January 10, 2019, joined by 42 Republican Senate cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee.
On July 22, 2020, the committee ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment; Senator Johnson formally reported it on December 14, 2020, with written report No. 116-311.

The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 614 on December 14, 2020, but the Senate never took it up, and no vote occurred before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Everyone covered by major federal rules is better off than they would have been under the bill: health, safety, environmental, and consumer protections continued to take effect under the existing process. Regulated industries did not get the congressional-approval requirement they sought.

for.name: Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 10, 2019, requiring congressional approval for major federal rules.

for.name: 42 of 53 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it the support of all but a handful of the Senate Republican conference.

for.name: Ron Johnson
for.role: Chair, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill favorably without amendment on December 14, 2020, sending it to the Senate calendar.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote after it was placed on the legislative calendar in December 2020; the Congress ended without action.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: The House, under Democratic control, took no action on the bill at any point in the 116th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsorship was Republican — Rand Paul plus 42 Republican cosponsors and a Republican-chaired committee that reported it — while Democratic-controlled bodies never acted on it, and it died without a recorded vote on either side.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel, chemical, and other major regulated manufacturers
industries.note: Rules costing $100 million or more a year would need an act of Congress to take effect, and most would die by default when Congress does nothing, giving polluting and hazardous industries a practical veto over environmental, safety, and public-health standards. Ordinary people would absorb the resulting exposure.

Consumer-protection and financial rules that meet the $100 million threshold would face the same approval requirement, making new investor and consumer safeguards far harder to put in place. The bill exempts only Federal Reserve monetary policy, not financial regulation generally.

Agencies would lose the ability to issue binding major rules on their own authority, and their scientific and economic justifications would be subject to a 70-day congressional clock. Weakening that authority weakens the government's ability to act on hazards that affect the public.
